note.text:
Computational thinking is a way of solving problems that computer scientists use. It has four parts: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms.
Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve, one at a time.
Example: organising a class party breaks into: decide the date and place; list what is needed; collect money and buy; decorate and prepare food; hold the party; clean up.
Advantages: each part is easier; different people can work on different parts; it is easier to find and fix mistakes.

worked_example.problem: Break the task “cook rice and stew for lunch” into smaller parts.
steps: Get the ingredients (rice, tomatoes, onions, oil, meat or fish).
Prepare them: wash the rice, cut the vegetables.
Cook the rice; cook the stew.
worked_example.answer: Get ingredients → prepare → cook → serve and wash up.

cards.idea: Decomposition is breaking a big problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve.
example: Writing a story: plan, write the beginning, the middle, the end, then check.

cards.idea: The small parts are solved one at a time, often in a sensible order.
example: You cannot clean up before the party.

cards.idea: Decomposition lets people share the work and makes mistakes easier to find.
example: One group decorates while another buys drinks.

right.text: Each small part is easier to solve.
Different people can work on different parts.

wrong.text: It means one person must do everything.
It removes the need to think.
wrong.explain: You still think about each part.
It makes mistakes easier to find.

right.text: breaking a big problem into smaller parts

wrong.text: ignoring details that do not matter
